# Getting started: make your folders in Bash

**Read this page first.** Log in to CREATE and open a terminal, following the
[course access instructions](https://zelezniak-lab.github.io/7BBG1002/create/rstudio_create.html).
Use your allocated working area on CREATE. All the work below takes place
remotely, not on your laptop.

We will use Unix to download yeast sequences, Conda and SeqKit to process them,
and R to make a table and figures. Your notebook will become your report.
Read each short explanation, run the commands, and answer the questions.

## Step 1: Create the directory structure

Run these commands in the **CREATE terminal**, one line at a time:

```{bash folders, eval=FALSE}
pwd
mkdir -p yeast_project
cd yeast_project
mkdir -p data/raw data/processed results/figures results/tables
ls
```

`pwd` shows where you are. `mkdir` creates a directory and `cd` moves into it.
The `-p` option creates any missing parent directories. `ls` lists the contents.
Your folder now looks like this:

```text
yeast_project/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/
│   └── processed/
└── results/
    ├── figures/
    └── tables/
```

Keep the original downloaded sequences in `raw`, the table you create in
`processed`, and your results in `results`. If you return to this practical
later, enter the existing `yeast_project` folder rather than creating it again.

# Exercise 1: Work with an RStudio Project

**Aim:** create a Project, use its working directory, and return to it later.
An RStudio Project connects RStudio to a folder containing your work. We will
use the `yeast_project` folder you already created in Bash.

In **remote RStudio**:

1. Select **File → New Project → Existing Directory**.

3. Open `analysis.Rmd` from the Files pane.

Check that the Project name appears at the top-right of RStudio. In the Files

# How to use this notebook

The **Console** runs R; the **Terminal** runs Bash. The notebook's code blocks
are called *chunks*. Run R chunks with the green arrow in their top-right corner.
Run the setup chunk near the top of the file first.

For the Bash steps below, copy the commands into the Terminal. They stay in your
notebook as a record, but have `eval=FALSE` so Knit will not reinstall software
or download the data again. R chunks run during knitting once the processed
table and tidyverse are available.

If needed, install the R packages **once in the R Console**:

```r
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "rmarkdown", "knitr"))
```

Project chunks are included when a `.Rproj` file is present beside this Rmd;
they are skipped when rendering the starter web page without a Project.

Try **Knit → Knit to HTML** now. The starter knits even before you answer the
questions or prepare data; analysis results will be added later. Do not put
unfinished R expressions in a chunk: leave your notes as comments beginning
with `#` until you are ready to write the code.

# Exercise 2: Download and inspect yeast sequences

We will use *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* coding sequences (CDS), from Ensembl
release 113, assembly R64-1-1. These are coding-sequence records, not whole
chromosomes or sequencing reads. Each record will become one row in our table.

## Step 1: Download the FASTA file

Run in the **Terminal**, from your project directory:

```{bash download-data, eval=FALSE}
wget -O data/raw/yeast_cds.fa.gz https://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-113/fasta/saccharomyces_cerevisiae/cds/Saccharomyces_cerevisiae.R64-1-1.cds.all.fa.gz
gzip -t data/raw/yeast_cds.fa.gz
```

The file is compressed, which is why its name ends in `.gz`. `gzip -t` checks
that it can be decompressed; no output means the check passed. The download URL
records exactly which release we used.

## Step 2: Look at the file

```{bash inspect-data, eval=FALSE}
zcat data/raw/yeast_cds.fa.gz | head
zcat data/raw/yeast_cds.fa.gz | grep -c '^>'
```

`zcat` reads compressed text. The pipe `|` sends it to another command.
`head` shows the first lines. In FASTA, each sequence starts with a header line
beginning with `>`; `grep -c '^>'` counts those headers.

**Questions:** How many sequence records are there? Why would counting all the
lines give a different answer?

**Answers:** _Write here._

# Exercise 3: Process the sequences with Conda and SeqKit

## Step 1: Create an environment

Conda keeps the software for this practical together. Use the course's
[Conda setup instructions](https://zelezniak-lab.github.io/7BBG1002/unix/conda_install.html)
if `conda` is not available, or ask the demonstrator.

Run this **once in the Terminal**. If you already have `yeast-tools`, skip the
creation command and run the version check.

```{bash conda-environment, eval=FALSE}
conda create -n yeast-tools --override-channels -c conda-forge -c bioconda seqkit=2.9.0 -y
conda run -n yeast-tools seqkit version
```

`-n` names the environment; `-c` chooses a package channel. We select a specific
SeqKit version so the software can be recorded and reused. `conda run` runs a
command inside that environment without needing to activate it in every chunk.

## Step 2: Summarise the FASTA

```{bash sequence-summary, eval=FALSE}
conda run -n yeast-tools seqkit stats data/raw/yeast_cds.fa.gz
```

**Question:** What are the shortest, longest and average sequence lengths?

**Answer:** _Write here._

## Step 3: Make a table for R

```{bash make-table, eval=FALSE}
printf 'record_id\tlength_bp\tgc_percent\n' > data/processed/yeast_cds.tsv
conda run -n yeast-tools seqkit fx2tab -n -i -l -g data/raw/yeast_cds.fa.gz >> data/processed/yeast_cds.tsv
head data/processed/yeast_cds.tsv
```

`fx2tab` converts the FASTA into a table. Here `-n` leaves out the sequence,
`-i` keeps the record ID, `-l` adds length, and `-g` adds GC percentage.
`printf` writes the column names; `\t` means a tab and `\n` means a new line.
`>` starts a file and `>>` adds to it. Run both lines together when rebuilding
the table, so you do not append the records twice.

**Question:** What does each of the three columns contain, and what are its units?

**Answer:** _Write here._

# Exercise 4: Explore the data in R

Return to the Rmd. **Run the setup chunk again**, then run the following chunks
in order. You can also click Knit: it runs the setup and R analysis in a fresh
session automatically. There are no settings to change in the header.

## Step 1: Read the table

```{r read-table, eval=analysis_ready}
yeast <- readr::read_tsv("data/processed/yeast_cds.tsv",
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
head(yeast)
nrow(yeast)
```

Check that the row count matches your FASTA count from Exercise 2.

## Step 2: Calculate a summary

```{r summary, eval=analysis_ready}
yeast_summary <- yeast %>%
  summarise(records = n(),
            mean_length = mean(length_bp),
            median_length = median(length_bp),
            mean_gc = mean(gc_percent))
yeast_summary
write_tsv(yeast_summary, "results/tables/summary.tsv")
```

`%>%` passes the data to the next operation. `summarise()` calculates summary
values. `write_tsv()` saves the result as a tab-separated table.

**Question:** Are mean and median length similar? What could explain a difference?

**Answer:** _Write here._

## Step 3: Select and sort records

```{r select-records, eval=analysis_ready}
long_cds <- yeast %>%
  filter(length_bp > 2000) %>%
  arrange(desc(length_bp))
head(long_cds)
```

`filter()` selects rows; `arrange()` sorts them. `desc()` puts the largest first.

# Exercise 5: Make figures with ggplot2

## Step 1: Plot the length distribution

```{r length-plot, eval=analysis_ready}
p_length <- ggplot(yeast, aes(x = length_bp)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "CDS length (bp)", y = "Number of records") +
  theme_minimal()
p_length
ggsave("results/figures/lengths.png", p_length, width = 8, height = 5)
```

`aes()` maps a column to an axis. `geom_histogram()` groups values into bins.
`labs()` labels the axes. `ggsave()` saves the figure, while printing `p_length`
puts it in the notebook and the HTML report.

**Your turn:** Copy and adapt this code to plot the GC percentage distribution.
Give the x-axis the correct label and save it under a different filename.

```{r your-gc-plot, eval=analysis_ready}
# Write your code here.
```

## Step 2: Compare length and GC

```{r scatter-plot, eval=analysis_ready}
ggplot(yeast, aes(x = length_bp, y = gc_percent)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "CDS length (bp)", y = "GC (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Questions:** What pattern do you see? What does `alpha = 0.3` change?
Try adding `+ scale_x_log10()` and describe how the plot changes.
